title: TraceBound: Evaluating Trace-Bounded Context for Token-Efficient Coding Agents

contributions.purpose: Test whether restricting agent file access to execution-trace-derived allowlists reduces token consumption.
contributions.mechanism: TraceBound, an inference-time framework that computes per-task file allowlists from failing-test execution traces (pytest coverage, depth-2 import closure, interface and auxiliary files) and gates agent file reads with hard denial of out-of-allowlist reads.
contributions.evaluation: Evaluated on FeatureBench Lite (30 feature development tasks) with OpenHands; TraceBound increases median input tokens by 25.72% (1.66M to 2.08M) rather than reducing them.
contributions.source_quote: TraceBound framework: An inference-time approach that derives file allowlists from test execution traces and enforces them during agent execution.

contributions.purpose: Characterize the file-navigation behavior of modern coding agents.
contributions.mechanism: Root cause analysis of denied read operations during TraceBound-gated agent runs on FeatureBench Lite.
contributions.evaluation: Only 2.3% of file reads fall outside trace-derived boundaries, showing agents already naturally focus on trace-relevant files.
contributions.source_quote: Empirical finding: Modern coding agents already exhibit focused file navigation behavior, with only 2.3% of reads falling outside trace-derived boundaries.

contributions.purpose: Report the negative result that binary file-access restriction cannot deliver token savings.
contributions.mechanism: Analysis concluding there is no headroom for restriction-based context reduction, while noting TraceBound improves average test pass rate by +5.76 percentage points, suggesting file-access guidance may still aid task completion.
contributions.evaluation: Median input tokens increase 25.72% instead of decreasing; pass rate improves +5.76 percentage points; future work pointed at content-level filtering.
contributions.source_quote: Negative result: Binary file-access restriction is insufficient for token reduction; future work should explore content-level filtering approaches.

self_declared_provenance.quote: This trace-bounded context approach differs from content-level pruning by enforcing a hard file-access constraint rather than compressing retrieved content.
This hard constraint differs from soft approaches like content pruning (Wang et al., 2026) in that it prevents irrelevant file reads entirely rather than compressing content after retrieval.

notes: Explicit negative-result paper: the core hypothesis fails (tokens increase 25.72% instead of decreasing; only 2.3% of reads denied). The paper self-labels its third contribution as a negative result; the +5.76pp pass-rate gain is a secondary positive side-effect.
